# Paint settings, swept

The [moving-hairs brush](paint_gestures.md) has many settings, and most of them interact. The
figures on this page each paint one gesture over and over, changing one setting from left to right
and keeping everything else as it is in the [black Elegy](paint_gestures.md#a-finished-piece): a
soft house painter's brush 10 cm wide, laying a thin film of fat black paint. Most settings are
taken well past their usual range, where they stop behaving and start doing something else. Where a
setting also belongs to an [ordinary brush](paint_canvas.md#brushes-made-to-order), a second row
paints the same path with one, at the same pressures. Click a figure to see it full size.

The gesture has four parts, top to bottom: a long straight stroke; a loop that crosses itself, so
the brush paints over its own wet paint; a scrub back and forth; and a last straight in four pieces,
each faster and lighter than the one before (100, 200, 350 and 600 mm/s) and lifting off the canvas
at the end. The code that paints it is
folded inside every example below; open it to see or change it. Each figure takes 10 to 20 seconds
to paint.

## The paint

How much paint the brush carries (`amount`, 1 is a full load) matters more than anything else
about the paint. A light load is a grey drawing of hair tracks; a full one is solid black; and a
brush loaded far past full stands its paint up in a thick crust where it first touches. The
ordinary brush goes the same way, but its black is a smooth silhouette with a tapered tail.

    val stiffness: Double = 0.5,
    val ragged: Double = 0.5,

    val stiff: Double = 0.5,
    val thinner: Double = 0.0,
    val oil: Double = 1.5,
    val amount: Double = 0.5,
    val hiding: Double = 0.65,
    val tilt: Double = 30.0,
    val faster: Double = 1.0,
    val facets: Double? = null,
    val moving: Boolean = true,
    val width: Double = 200.0,
    val hair: Double? = null,
    val cohesion: Double? = null,

// A canvas 50 cm wide and 1.25 m tall; the default brush is 10 cm wide.
fun canvas() = PaintCanvas(300, aspect = 0.4, groundColor = rgb(0.93, 0.9, 0.83), sizeMm = 500.0, seed = 7)
val straight = FLine().moveTo(500, 120).lineTo(510, 900)
val loop = FLine().moveTo(510, 900).apply {
    for (i in 1..480) {
        val a = PI / 2 + 2 * PI * 1.15 * i / 480
        lineTo(510 + 190 * cos(a), 1090 - 190 * sin(a))
    }
}
val scrub =
    FLine().moveTo(560, 1330).apply { for (i in 0 until 5) lineTo(if (i % 2 == 0) 380.0 else 640.0, 1375.0 + 45 * i) }
val last =
    [1600.0, 1800.0, 2000.0, 2200.0, 2400.0].zipWithNext().mapIndexed { k, (y0, y1) ->
        FLine().moveTo(500.0 + 4 * k, y0).lineTo(504.0 + 4 * k, y1)
    }

// a long straight, a loop that crosses itself, a scrub back and forth, and a last straight in four
// pieces, each faster and lighter: 100, 200, 350, then 600 mm/s, lifting off the canvas at the end
fun gesture(c: PaintCanvas, s: Settings): TimedGesture {
    fun part(line: FLine, speed: Double, vararg pressure: Double) =
        c.gesture(line, speed = speed, pressure = pressure.toList(), tilt = s.tilt, facets = s.facets)
    var g =
        part(straight, 250.0, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0).then(part(loop, 250.0, 1.0, 0.9)).pause(0.1).then(part(scrub, 300.0, 1.1))
    val press = [1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.3, -0.2]
    for ((k, speed) in [100.0, 200.0, 350.0, 600.0].withIndex()) g =
        g.then(part(last[k], speed, press[k], press[k + 1]))
    return g.faster(s.faster)
}

fun column(label: String, s: Settings): Pair<String, Img> {
    val c = canvas()
    if (s.absorbent > 0.0) c.prime(rgb(0.93, 0.9, 0.83), texture = 0.0, absorbent = s.absorbent)
    val config = BrushConfig(
        bristles = s.bristles,
        hair = s.hair,
        stiffness = s.stiffness,
        ragged = s.ragged,
        splay = s.splay,
        lay = s.lay,
        run = s.run,
        pickup = s.pickup,
        push = s.push,
    )
    val black = rgb(0.05, 0.045, 0.04)
    if (s.moving) {
        val brush =
            c.dynamicBrush(BrushKind.HogFlat, s.width, hairs = s.hairs, segments = 6, config = config)
                .load(
                    black,
                    hiding = s.hiding,
                    stiff = s.stiff,
                    drying = s.drying,
                    thinner = s.thinner,
                    oil = s.oil,
                    amount = s.amount,
                )
        brush.set(cohesion = s.cohesion, clumping = s.clumping, splayFan = s.splayFan, splayScatter = s.splayScatter)
        c.stroke(gesture(c, s), brush)
    } else {
        // an ordinary brush along the same path, with the same pressures; it has no timing or tilt
        val brush =
            c.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, s.width, config = config)
                .load(
                    black,
                    hiding = s.hiding,
                    stiff = s.stiff,
                    drying = s.drying,
                    thinner = s.thinner,
                    oil = s.oil,
                    amount = s.amount,
                )
        c.stroke(straight, brush, pressure = 0.8..1.0)
        c.stroke(loop, brush, pressure = 1.0..0.9)
        c.stroke(scrub, brush, pressure = 1.1..1.1)
        c.stroke(FLine().moveTo(500, 1600).lineTo(516, 2400), brush, pressure = 1.0..0.0)
    }
    // a rag wiped across the bar, the loop and the last stroke after some minutes (infinite: dry first)
    s.wipeAfter?.let { minutes ->
        if (minutes.isInfinite()) c.dry() else c.wait(minutes)
        val rag = c.rag(150.0)
        for (y in [500.0, 1090.0, 2000.0]) c.wipe(FLine().moveTo(250, y).lineTo(760, y + 10), rag, [0.8])
    }
    if (s.dry) c.dry()
    val png = if (s.lamp) c.png(relief = 0.3, light = PaintLight.Gallery) else c.png(relief = 0.3)
    return label to imgFromBytes(png).also { c.close() }
}

// the same columns twice: a row with moving hairs above a row with an ordinary brush
fun rows(cells: (moving: Boolean) -> List<Pair<String, Img>>): Img {
    val rows =
        ["moving hairs" to true, "ordinary brush" to false].map { (name, moving) ->
            val strokes = cells(moving)
            name to montage(strokes, columns = strokes.size, cellSide = 750, textScale = 3)
        }
    return montage(rows, columns = 1, cellSide = 4000, textScale = 3)
}

`lay` (in `BrushConfig`) is how thick a film a full brush lays. Thin, the bristle tracks show
through the black; thick, they disappear, and far past the usual the paint spreads into one solid
silhouette, lumpy where the bar starts. The ordinary brush is solid black from 2.

loop; very long, it never runs out and the gesture is one solid shape. Both brushes run out alike.

A little painting medium (`thinner`, a share of the paint's volume) changes the black all at once.
Up to about 0.01 the film still covers; from 0.02 it breaks into streaks with dark outlines, and
then into a pale veil over the ground; and at 0.9 the paint is nearly all medium and almost nothing
stays. The ordinary brush holds its black a little longer, to about 0.05.

the hairs are rigid rods that splinter the loop and the scrub into hard straight marks. The ordinary
brush hardly notices: from 1 up its scrub spreads a little wider and its last stroke parts at the top.

The moving hairs' clumping comes in two models, and `clumping` (set on the brush:
`brush.set(clumping = ...)`) blends between them. At 0, as a brush is made, the liquid draws the tips
of hairs that are neighbours at the root together. At 1 it joins any two wet hairs that come near
each other with a bridge of paint, which pulls them together and snaps when they are pulled a few
spacings apart, so the brush gathers into clumps that splay can tear apart, and the bristles they
carry gather with them. Between, the two pull together; past 1 the bridges pull harder, and below 0
the old model pulls harder while the bridges push. The sweep runs from -1 to 2 at cohesion 4,
unsplayed and at splay 2.

`splay` pushes every pressed hair straight out from the brush's middle, so a flat can only part in
two. `splayFan` 1 pushes each in proportion to how far out its root is, so the brush fans open and
neighbours part everywhere; `splayScatter` turns each push off the outward by its own slowly drifting
angle and amount, alike for hairs near each other, the way pressed hairs buckle in bundles. With
liquid bridges, the bundles hold together and each leaves its own trail, braiding and crossing.

# A solid, written down: `afield.lang.solidsl` In `afield.lang.solidsl` a shape is a **value**. Subtracting a cylinder from a cuboid builds an expression tree, and from that one tree you can march a mesh, build an exact CSG solid, emit GLSL, or simplify it. A document you can open and run is [at the bottom of the page](#open-this); the KDoc for `SolidExpr`, `Profile`, `SolidLowering` and `SolidTemplate` covers every declaration used here. The signed-distance vocabulary in `mesh_sdf.kt` works the other way round. It declares ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} typealias ScalarField3D = (Vec3) -> Float ``` and builds its primitives and combinators on top of it: `sdfSphere`, `sdfBox`, `sdfTorus`, `sdfUnion`, `sdfSmoothUnion`, `twisted`, `repeated`. Every one of them returns a Kotlin lambda, and a lambda cannot be printed, compared, serialized, rewritten, or emitted as GLSL. [RectSL](rectsl_examples.md)'s 2D tracks are expression trees for that reason, and SolidSL does the same in three dimensions. Here is one part, and the four things you can ask of it: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val part = (cuboid(4, 2.6, 0.7) + cylinder(1.4, 0.8)) - cylinder(3.0, 0.42) - Profile.rect(2.9, 0.85).offset(0.22).extruded(3.0).at(0, 1.05, -1.5) part.toScalarField() // (Vec3) -> Float — marchable, and everything mesh_sdf.kt does part.exactSolid() // Manifold's exact CSG — a guaranteed-closed Solid, or a stated refusal part.toGlsl() // float sdSolid(vec3 p) — a real-time raymarch of the same source part.simplified() // a smaller expression that means the same thing println(part) // Difference(children=[Union(children=[Cuboid(x=4.0, … ``` ## The vocabulary Solids, booleans, transforms, and a 2D `Profile` you sweep into the third dimension. Everything else in the package reads a tree built from these.
| Example | Behavior | | --- | --- | | `sphere(1.0)` | Constructs a sphere centred on the origin. Its radius uses the same coordinate units as the rest of the expression. | | `cuboid(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)` / `cuboid(1.0)` | Constructs an origin-centred box from full extents, or a cube from one side length. Dimensions are not half-extents. | | `cylinder(2.0, 0.5, 0.25)` / `cone(2.0, 0.5)` | Builds a cylinder or frustum along z, centred on the origin. The cone is the zero-top-radius case, with its tip at positive half-height. | | `torus(1.0, 0.2)` | Revolves a circular tube around the z axis, with the ring in the XY plane. The major radius is the ring radius and the minor radius is the tube radius. | | `gyroid(3.0, 0.2)` | Defines an unbounded gyroid sheet field. Intersect it with a finite shape before expecting a bounded object. | | `Profile.circle(0.5)` / `Profile.rect(1.0, 0.5)` | Builds a two-dimensional circular or rectangular profile. Extrude or revolve it to create a solid. | | `Profile.star(5, 1.0, 0.4)` / `Profile.polygon(points)` | Builds a star from alternating radii or a polygon from supplied points. The profile can then enter the same sweep and Boolean operations. | | `profile.offset(0.1)` | Offsets the profile boundary before a sweep. Use a profile offset when the two-dimensional cross-section is what should grow. | | `profile.translated(1.0, 0.0).turned(30.0)` | Moves and rotates the profile in its plane. Rotation is in degrees. | | `profile.sized(2.0)` | Scales a profile before extrusion or revolution. This changes the cross-section rather than the later solid’s height. | | `profile.extruded(2.0, twistDegrees = 45.0)` | Sweeps the profile through the given height with optional twist in degrees. The result is a three-dimensional expression. | | `profile.revolved(360.0)` | Revolves a profile through the supplied angle in degrees. A full turn closes the revolution around its axis. | | `shape.at(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)` | Translates a solid expression by the given displacement. The source expression is retained as a child of the transform. | | `shape.turned(0.0, 0.0, 45.0)` | Rotates about the origin using Euler angles in degrees, applied x then y then z. Translation order therefore matters. | | `shape.sized(2.0)` / `shape.sized(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)` | Scales uniformly or separately along each axis. Use the uniform form when proportions should remain unchanged. | | `shape.mirrored(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)` | Reflects across the plane specified by its normal. This reverses the side of the shape along that normal. | | `shape.rounded(0.1)` / `shape.shelled(0.1)` | Rounds the field boundary outward by `0.1`, or creates a shell with wall thickness `0.2` (twice the argument). These field operations require sampled lowering when the exact backend cannot represent them. | | `a + b` / `a - b` / `a and b` | Forms union, ordered subtraction or intersection. The same Boolean spellings apply to profiles; subtraction removes b from a. | | `unionOf(listOf(a, b, c))` / `differenceOf(listOf(a, b, c))` / `intersectionOf(listOf(a, b, c))` | Combines more than two solids in one expression. Difference preserves the first shape and removes the later shapes. | | `smoothUnion(a, b, 0.2)` / `smoothDifference(a, b, 0.2)` | Blends field boundaries with the supplied smoothing scale. Neither is a superset of the other, so which one you want depends on what you are going to do next:
| Property | `toScalarField()` | `exactSolid()` | |---|---|---| | what the shape becomes | a distance field, sampled on a grid | a CSG tree, evaluated exactly | | how a surface appears | marching cubes, `O(h²)` | it **is** the surface | | a cylinder is | a true cylinder | an inscribed *n*-gon prism | | a smooth blend is | native | **refused**, with a reason | | a gyroid is | native | **refused** | | runs on a GPU | yes, via `toGlsl()` | no | | safe to subtract from | not reliably | always |
The practical consequence is a rule about which knob to turn. On the exact path the mesh is as coarse as the shape allows — a flat face is two triangles, an L-bracket cut from a plate is **20 triangles** where the marched version of the same expression is 71,288 — and refining the march does nothing at all, because there is no march. What you turn there is `segments`. On the field path, refining the march improves a polyhedral shape and bottoms out on a curved one at Manifold's faceting floor, so past a certain point you are paying for triangles that buy nothing. `crossCheck` builds a shape both ways and compares volume, area, genus and a symmetric Hausdorff distance, which is how the two are held to each other; [`dev_docs/SOLIDSL_AGREEMENT.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/SOLIDSL_AGREEMENT.md) records what that costs and where the floors are. ## Refusals are in the type `exactSolid()` does not return a `Solid`. It returns a `SolidLowering`, which is either the solid or a refusal carrying a sentence about why, following `RectSLFnLowering`'s convention: a `null` invites a caller to substitute something plausible, and an exception loses the reason at the first `runCatching`. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} when (val l = shape.exactSolid()) { is SolidLowering.Lowered -> println("volume ${l.value.volume}, genus ${l.value.genus}") is SolidLowering.Refused -> println("no exact form: ${l.why}") } ``` There are two flavours: | node | why | flavour | |---|---|---| | `SmoothUnion`, `SmoothDifference` | the fillet surface lies on **neither** operand, so no union, intersection or difference of the two can produce it | permanent | | `Gyroid` | a trigonometric field on all of space, not a bounded volume | permanent | | `Round` | `minkowskiSum` with a sphere *exists* — but that sphere is an inscribed polyhedron, so the result is strictly inside the true offset by up to its sagitta, and **refining the march does not close a gap that is not the march's** | would not converge | | `Shell` | a grow minus an erode: `Round`'s error twice over, with a concave decomposition between them | would not converge | The difference between the flavours is whether an exact-looking answer exists. A permanent refusal has none. A would-not-converge refusal has one available and it is wrong by up to the sagitta of a polyhedral ball, in a direction refining the march cannot close. The emitted code is straight-line, single-assignment and entirely scalar — no `vec3` locals, no swizzles, no loops. GPU drivers re-vectorise it anyway, and code that plain is easy to parse back, which is how the emitter is tested. Read `GlslSolid.stepScale` before you trace with it. Sphere tracing is only safe where the field is a lower bound on the true distance, and several nodes break that: `Intersect` and `Difference` are pointwise maxima, and a twisted `Extrude` shears space. The emitter reports `1.0`, `0.7` or `0.4` with the offending node named; multiply your march step by it. ## The simplifier Most of `simplified()` is housekeeping any algebra accumulates the moment somebody generates code into it: identity transforms drop, adjacent translations fold, nested booleans of one kind flatten into a single n-ary node — which matters here because n-ary is what reaches Manifold's *batch* boolean rather than a fold of *n−1* nested ones. Two rules go further, and both need a tree rather than a closure. **Duplicate operands collapse**, because two `SolidExpr.Sphere(1.0)` are `==` where two `sdfSphere(1.0)` closures are different objects forever. And **an operand that cannot reach the body is dropped**, decided from symbolic bounds: on a plate with fifty bores of which three actually meet it, the emitted shader goes from **610 statements to 46**. One rule can change which backend you get. `SmoothUnion(a, b, k = 0)` *is* a union, and a union has an exact CSG form where a smooth blend never will, so simplifying can move an expression off the level-set fallback and onto the exact path: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} println(smoothUnion(a, b, k = 0.0).simplificationReport()) // nodes 3 -> 1, GLSL 19 -> 10 statements, path level set -> exact ``` Three rewrites are refused, so do not expect them: composing two general Euler rotations (a matrix does not always come back out as three angles), reassociating `SmoothUnion`, reordering a `Difference`. The last two are simply not associative and not commutative. ## Solving for the numbers A tree you can read is also a tree you can differentiate, and that is the third thing you can do with one source. Declare which numbers in a shape are free, hand over some samples of the shape you actually want, and a gradient finds them — the 3D version of what [`afield.lang.rectsl.RectSLFn`](rectsl_inverse_animation.md) does for 2D tracks. The machinery is `afield.math.autodiff.AD`, reverse-mode automatic differentiation over `Double`: `SolidGradient.kt` is `SolidField.kt`'s `toField3` transposed line for line into `AD` arithmetic. Reverse mode because the objective is one scalar loss over many sample points and a handful of parameters, so one forward pass and one backward sweep give every parameter derivative at once. The position gradient falls off the same tape for free, which is what makes the fitted result still a field you can march. ### Naming the numbers A `SolidExpr` is an anonymous tree of `data class`es with no names anywhere in it. A parameter is bound instead to a **structural address**: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val part = smoothUnion(sphere(0.45), cylinder(1.90, 0.16), k = 0.18) part.numericSlots() // SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius = 0.45 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.height = 1.9 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.radiusLow = 0.16 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.radiusHigh = 0.16 // SmoothUnion.k = 0.18 val template = part.parameterize { param("sphereRadius", "SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius") param("barHeight", "SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.height") param("barRadius") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field.startsWith("radius") } // both, tied }.orThrow() template.gradientAt(0.9, 0.0, 0.0, template.seed) // value 0.450000 dPos 1.000, 0.000, 0.000 dParam -1.000, 0.000, 0.000 ``` `barRadius` drives **two** slots, which is how a symmetry constraint is written: "the bar is a cylinder, not a frustum", in the parameterisation rather than in a comment. A fit over two independently-varying radii and a fit over one shared radius are different problems and the notation should be able to say which is meant. `segments` is missing from that list, and cannot be fitted. `toScalarField()` ignores it entirely — a `Sphere`'s field is a true sphere whatever its `segments` says — and the exact lowering consumes it as a count of polygon sides, where its effect is a jump. Neither has a derivative with respect to it. ### What `parameterize` refuses Differentiating refuses nothing: every node with a field form has a gradient form, because `AD` is closed over everything `Field3` uses. It is *binding a parameter* that can be refused, and the refusals fall into three groups you can act on: - **the address is wrong** — a path that does not resolve, a predicate that matched nothing, or no `param(…)` call at all. The message lists the slots that *do* exist, so `numericSlots()` and the refusal tell you the same thing from either end. - **two names, one number** — a name declared twice, two names claiming the same slot, or one name tying slots that currently hold different values, which would make the seed ambiguous. - **the seed is singular before the first step** — a `Scale` factor at zero (the field divides by it and the derivative goes as `1/s²`) or a blend `k` at zero (its field clamps at `1e-9`, below which the blend is a hard boolean with no derivative in `k`, so the parameter would never move). Which nodes are *good* to fit is the inverse of which nodes lower exactly: | node | `toScalarField` | `exactSolid` | the gradient | |---|---|---|---| | `SmoothUnion` | native | **refused** — the fillet lies on neither operand | native, and **C¹**: no kink at all | | `SmoothDifference` | native | **refused** | native, C¹ | | `Gyroid` | native | **refused** — not a bounded volume | native; one `abs` kink on the mid-sheet | | `Round` | native | **refused** — would not converge | native, exactly `f − r` | | `Union` | native | native | a subgradient on the seam, split 0.5/0.5 | The two nodes the exact kernel refuses outright are the two the gradient handles best, so if a shape is going to be fitted, write it with `smoothUnion` and `smoothDifference`. `gradientNotes()` says which of these apply to your own expression, beside `fieldNotes()` and `allRefusals()`. ### Where the gradient has a kink A distance field is full of kinks: `min` and `max` *are* CSG, `abs` is `Shell` and `Gyroid`, `sqrt` at zero is every radial primitive's own centre. `abs`, `min` and `max` split the derivative **0.5/0.5 at an exact tie**, so a sample that lands exactly where two CSG children meet gets half the gradient from each side rather than an arbitrary one of them, and the step it takes still decreases the loss. `gradientNotes()` also flags the two places a smaller step cannot help. At a radial primitive's own centre `√·` has an infinite derivative, so a sample there gives `Infinity` in the *position* gradient and `NaN` as soon as it meets a zero: sample away from centres, or use the parameter gradient, which is finite there. And a parameter that only feeds an empty subtree, or a `segments` count, has derivative exactly zero for every value, so a descent on it reports convergence immediately. Subtracting a cylinder from a cuboid builds an expression tree, and from that one tree you can march a mesh, build an exact CSG solid, emit GLSL, or simplify it. A document you can open and run is [at the bottom of the page](#open-this); the KDoc for `SolidExpr`, `Profile`, `SolidLowering` and `SolidTemplate` covers every declaration used here. The signed-distance vocabulary in `mesh_sdf.kt` works the other way round. It declares ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} typealias ScalarField3D = (Vec3) -> Float ``` and builds its primitives and combinators on top of it: `sdfSphere`, `sdfBox`, `sdfTorus`, `sdfUnion`, `sdfSmoothUnion`, `twisted`, `repeated`. Every one of them returns a Kotlin lambda, and a lambda cannot be printed, compared, serialized, rewritten, or emitted as GLSL. [RectSL](rectsl_examples.md)'s 2D tracks are expression trees for that reason, and SolidSL does the same in three dimensions. Everything else in the package reads a tree built from these.
| Example | Behavior | | --- | --- | | `sphere(1.0)` | Constructs a sphere centred on the origin. Its radius uses the same coordinate units as the rest of the expression. | | `cuboid(2.0, 1.0, 0.5)` / `cuboid(1.0)` | Constructs an origin-centred box from full extents, or a cube from one side length. Dimensions are not half-extents. | | `cylinder(2.0, 0.5, 0.25)` / `cone(2.0, 0.5)` | Builds a cylinder or frustum along z, centred on the origin. GPU drivers re-vectorise it anyway, and code that plain is easy to parse back, which is how the emitter is tested. Read `GlslSolid.stepScale` before you trace with it. Two rules go further, and both need a tree rather than a closure. **Duplicate operands collapse**, because two `SolidExpr.Sphere(1.0)` are `==` where two `sdfSphere(1.0)` closures are different objects forever. And **an operand that cannot reach the body is dropped**, decided from symbolic bounds: on a plate with fifty bores of which three actually meet it, the emitted shader goes from **610 statements to 46**. One rule can change which backend you get. `SmoothUnion(a, b, k = 0)` *is* a union, and a union has an exact CSG form where a smooth blend never will, so simplifying can move an expression off the level-set fallback and onto the exact path: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} println(smoothUnion(a, b, k = 0.0).simplificationReport()) // nodes 3 -> 1, GLSL 19 -> 10 statements, path level set -> exact ``` Three rewrites are refused, so do not expect them: composing two general Euler rotations (a matrix does not always come back out as three angles), reassociating `SmoothUnion`, reordering a `Difference`. The last two are simply not associative and not commutative. ## Solving for the numbers A tree you can read is also a tree you can differentiate, and that is the third thing you can do with one source. Declare which numbers in a shape are free, hand over some samples of the shape you actually want, and a gradient finds them — the 3D version of what [`afield.lang.rectsl.RectSLFn`](rectsl_inverse_animation.md) does for 2D tracks. The machinery is `afield.math.autodiff.AD`, reverse-mode automatic differentiation over `Double`: `SolidGradient.kt` is `SolidField.kt`'s `toField3` transposed line for line into `AD` arithmetic. Reverse mode because the objective is one scalar loss over many sample points and a handful of parameters, so one forward pass and one backward sweep give every parameter derivative at once. The position gradient falls off the same tape for free, which is what makes the fitted result still a field you can march. ### Naming the numbers A `SolidExpr` is an anonymous tree of `data class`es with no names anywhere in it. A parameter is bound instead to a **structural address**: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val part = smoothUnion(sphere(0.45), cylinder(1.90, 0.16), k = 0.18) part.numericSlots() // SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius = 0.45 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.height = 1.9 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.radiusLow = 0.16 // SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.radiusHigh = 0.16 // SmoothUnion.k = 0.18 val template = part.parameterize { param("sphereRadius", "SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius") param("barHeight", "SmoothUnion/b/Cylinder.height") param("barRadius") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field.startsWith("radius") } // both, tied }.orThrow() template.gradientAt(0.9, 0.0, 0.0, template.seed) // value 0.450000 dPos 1.000, 0.000, 0.000 dParam -1.000, 0.000, 0.000 ``` `barRadius` drives **two** slots, which is how a symmetry constraint is written: "the bar is a cylinder, not a frustum", in the parameterisation rather than in a comment. A fit over two independently-varying radii and a fit over one shared radius are different problems and the notation should be able to say which is meant. `segments` is missing from that list, and cannot be fitted. `toScalarField()` ignores it entirely — a `Sphere`'s field is a true sphere whatever its `segments` says — and the exact lowering consumes it as a count of polygon sides, where its effect is a jump. Neither has a derivative with respect to it. ### What `parameterize` refuses Differentiating refuses nothing: every node with a field form has a gradient form, because `AD` is closed over everything `Field3` uses. It is *binding a parameter* that can be refused, and the refusals fall into three groups you can act on: - **the address is wrong** — a path that does not resolve, a predicate that matched nothing, or no `param(…)` call at all. The message lists the slots that *do* exist, so `numericSlots()` and the refusal tell you the same thing from either end. - **two names, one number** — a name declared twice, two names claiming the same slot, or one name tying slots that currently hold different values, which would make the seed ambiguous. - **the seed is singular before the first step** — a `Scale` factor at zero (the field divides by it and the derivative goes as `1/s²`) or a blend `k` at zero (its field clamps at `1e-9`, below which the blend is a hard boolean with no derivative in `k`, so the parameter would never move). Which nodes are *good* to fit is the inverse of which nodes lower exactly: | node | `toScalarField` | `exactSolid` | the gradient | |---|---|---|---| | `SmoothUnion` | native | **refused** — the fillet lies on neither operand | native, and **C¹**: no kink at all | | `SmoothDifference` | native | **refused** | native, C¹ | | `Gyroid` | native | **refused** — not a bounded volume | native; one `abs` kink on the mid-sheet | | `Round` | native | **refused** — would not converge | native, exactly `f − r` | | `Union` | native | native | a subgradient on the seam, split 0.5/0.5 | The two nodes the exact kernel refuses outright are the two the gradient handles best, so if a shape is going to be fitted, write it with `smoothUnion` and `smoothDifference`. `gradientNotes()` says which of these apply to your own expression, beside `fieldNotes()` and `allRefusals()`. ### Where the gradient has a kink A distance field is full of kinks: `min` and `max` *are* CSG, `abs` is `Shell` and `Gyroid`, `sqrt` at zero is every radial primitive's own centre. `abs`, `min` and `max` split the derivative **0.5/0.5 at an exact tie**, so a sample that lands exactly where two CSG children meet gets half the gradient from each side rather than an arbitrary one of them, and the step it takes still decreases the loss. `gradientNotes()` also flags the two places a smaller step cannot help. At a radial primitive's own centre `√·` has an infinite derivative, so a sample there gives `Infinity` in the *position* gradient and `NaN` as soon as it meets a zero: sample away from centres, or use the parameter gradient, which is finite there. And a parameter that only feeds an empty subtree, or a `segments` count, has derivative exactly zero for every value, so a descent on it reports convergence immediately. A child that is nowhere nearest (a small sphere swallowed inside a large one) receives exactly `0.0` from every sample, and a descent on its radius stops immediately because the gradient really is zero. ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} unionOf([sphere(1.0), sphere(0.25)]).parameterize { … } .fitParameters(target, …).deadParameters // [inner] smoothUnion(sphere(1.0), sphere(0.25), k = 0.9).parameterize { … } .fitParameters(target, …).deadParameters // [] ``` `SolidFit.deadParameters` names the parameters whose gradient was exactly zero at the start, and those the descent never moved off their seed. Nothing in it wants the interior filled, so a shape that puts *some* surface through the points scores as well as the one that generated them. A cloud that surrounds a closed surface pins it from every side and recovers well; crop it to one hemisphere and every parameter that only shows itself on the missing side wanders freely, with the loss never going up. `Shell` and `Round` are riskier here than under `fitParameters` for the same reason: `abs(f) − t` is zero on two surfaces, so a shell can satisfy a cloud with the wrong one. `SolidCloudFit.unconstrainedParameters` is the point-cloud analogue of `deadParameters` and exists for the same reason — the failure arrives looking like convergence. #### A one-sided view Here the target is three lobes in a row, each with its own radius, and the cloud is cropped to `x < 0.10`, as a scanner looking from one side would see it. Everything else follows Manifold's conventions unchanged: - `cylinder` runs along **Z**. - `Profile.extruded(h)` runs from `z = 0` to `z = h` — *not* centred, because `Section.extruded` is not. - `Profile.revolved()` turns about **Z**, profile at `x ≥ 0`, counter-clockwise from `+X`. The mesh lathe `revolveMesh` defaults to Y; pass `axis = RevolveAxis.Z` to get the same solid from it. - `turned(x, y, z)` is in **degrees**, applied X then Y then Z. There is no `Torus` node: `torus(R, r)` is a function that builds `Profile.circle(r).translated(R, 0).revolved()`, which is what a torus is. ## Open this {#open-this} The [`solidsl_gallery`](agent_transcripts.md#solidsl_gallery) starting point has three boxes.
